deep_dive.title: Control of Seizure Dynamics in a Bistable System with Pulsatile Inputs
deep_dive.abstract: Bistable neural population models describe transitions associated with epilepsy through the coexistence of a stable equilibrium representing normal neural activity and a stable limit cycle representing seizure-like oscillations. Perturbations that drive the system outside the equilibrium's basin of attraction can trigger transitions to seizure-like activity. Enlarging this basin enables the system to recover normal activity from a larger set of perturbed states, providing a model-based mechanism for reducing frequency of seizure initiation. Motivated by electrical brain stimulation, this paper investigates basin enlargement using pulsatile feedback control. Combining higher-order averaging with periodic near-identity transformations, we establish conditions under which nonzero-mean and zero-mean pulsatile feedback gains enlarge the basin of attraction and derive guidelines for pulse design. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical enlargement.

quick_skim.title: Recognition of auditory objects from continuous and ultra-sparse spike streams in neuromorphic devices
quick_skim.abstract: Energy consumption is a major concern for modern artificial intelligence (AI) applications. The brain is thought to achieve energy-efficient computation through sparse coding schemes. By emulating the spiking dynamics of the brain, neuromorphic chips hold the potential to realize energy-efficient AI. In this work, we use birdsong to demonstrate that auditory object recognition can be achieved using ultra-sparse coding. Feature-detecting neurons tuned to short temporal features ($\sim$37 ms), sampled from exemplar syllables, transform continuous auditory signals into streams of ultra-sparse spikes that mark the onsets and offsets of features within the signal. Spike patterns elicited by the exemplars are stored as templates. During recognition, template matching is performed using axonal delays between feature-detecting and template-detecting neurons. Recognition is further enhanced by an additional group of specialized binary neurons trained to discriminate between syllable categories with subtle differences. When tested on Bengalese finch songs, our approach achieved error rates below 5% using 10 to 40 exemplars per syllable type. We then implemented this recognition algorithm using spiking neural networks on Intel's neuromorphic chip, Loihi, and found that response latencies remain constant (approximately 17 ms per syllable), regardless of the number of templates used. Our results demonstrate the potential of neuromorphic chips for low-latency, low-energy recognition of complex sounds, including speech.

quick_skim.title: Dynamical mean-field theory for associative memory with block-correlated patterns
quick_skim.abstract: In associative memories storing correlated patterns, retrieval of individual memories can compete with symmetric mixed states. A dynamical description is needed to determine how the initial state selects between these outcomes. We extend the generating-functional dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for independent patterns to independent blocks of correlated binary patterns of fixed finite size. The resulting effective single-neuron process has a self-consistent cross-talk noise covariance and self-feedback coefficients that depend on the block-covariance eigenvalues. For hierarchically correlated patterns with nonmonotonic transfer, increasing the loading can permit retrieval from an imperfect initial state before further loading prevents it. DMFT reproduces the retrieval trajectories and basin geometry found in direct simulations. Near the lower boundary of this re-entrant region, direct networks reveal stationary saddles separating coexisting mixed and target-retrieval states. Parameter sensitivities of DMFT trajectories predict nearby shifts of this boundary. At the tested upper boundary, retrieval remains accessible from initial states with larger target overlap, indicating a change in basin access. Under fixed-point convergence assumptions, the theory recovers the equations of generalized self-consistent signal-to-noise analysis.

quick_skim.title: A Pretrained Model for Bayesian Filtering in Heterogeneous Dynamical Systems
quick_skim.abstract: Filtering has not yet had its foundation-model moment: state estimation is still dominated either by online Bayesian filtering algorithms that require known dy- namics as inputs, or by learning-based neural filters trained from scratch for a single system or parametric family. The core challenge is structural heterogene- ity: dynamical systems differ in their governing dynamics, physical scales, and noise levels, precluding a shared representation space for a reusable filter. To bridge this gap, we introduce FilterFM, the first pretrained model for Bayesian filtering that estimates latent states across heterogeneous dynamical systems with a single checkpoint. FilterFM employs a hierarchical two-level observation se- quence encoder and a prior-to-posterior state-reconstruction module that together handle varying observation and state dimensions across heterogeneous systems, while modeling state uncertainty via quantile prediction. Trained on a mixture of heterogeneous filtering tasks, FilterFM exhibits superior in-domain performance, delivering significant gains in estimation accuracy, runtime efficiency, and noise robustness compared to existing baselines. Beyond in-domain performance, it marks the first model to successfully enable zero-shot filtering on unseen dynamics, bridging the generalization gap in state estimation. Furthermore, we uncover clear scaling behaviors in foundation-model-based Bayesian filtering, which combined with comprehensive component ablation studies, validate the structural optimality of our design and broaden the generalization scope for this research field.
quick_skim.llm_evidence_en: pretrained Bayesian filtering for state estimation applicable to neural decoding
